t: #2980 Check if Bitwise OR Has Trailing Zeros
o: An OR has a trailing zero exactly when its last binary bit is 0, i.e., the result is even. OR-ing numbers yields an even number iff at least one operand is even. So the question reduces to: can we pick two or more elements such that at least one is even — equivalently, are there at least two even numbers (we need two or more selected elements overall)? Example 1 has evens 2 and 4 → true. Example 2 is all even → true. Example 3 is all odd → false, since any OR of odd numbers stays odd.
k: OR preserves evenness possibility: the result is even iff at least one selected element is even.
Selecting two or more elements containing an even number is possible iff the count of even numbers is at least 2.
Any subset of size ≥ 2 with an even OR must contain an even element, which alone can be paired with anything else.

a.i: Directly try every pair and check whether its OR is even. Correct because if any larger subset works, some pair inside it also works (the even member paired with any other element keeps the OR even).
s: Double loop over all index pairs i < j.
Return true immediately if the OR is even; return false after all pairs.
a.t: O(n^2) — all pairs examined in the worst case (n ≤ 100)

a.i: The OR of a selection is even iff some selected element is even. We need at least two selected elements, so the answer is simply whether at least two even numbers exist.

w: Always present the parity observation first; the one-liner is the expected answer. Pitfall: thinking you need to simulate ORs of large subsets — parity makes it unnecessary. Follow-ups: what about trailing zeros in other bases, or requiring the OR to be divisible by 4 (then count numbers divisible by 4, or combinations whose low bits supply the needed zeros)?
